sub_scenario.family: rapid live troubleshooting leadership versus careful asynchronous incident analysis
sub_scenario.one_line: medical device vigilance analyst: rank evidence synthesis above hazard spokesperson

dialogue.content: I spent the first hour tidying the complaint chronology and closing stale entries.
Anything still open?
Two items, both with owners.
The safety inbox review wrapped early today.
Any surprises in it?
None worth recording.
I presented a completed complaint chronology to quality last week.
Was the cause still disputed?
No, the review had already closed.
Someone new shadowed me in the vigilance office this morning.
Did that slow you down?
A little, but the questions were good ones.
I batched my replies about the recall alerts into one message before lunch.
Cleaner than drip-feeding answers.
Much cleaner.
For a February pump-alarm cluster, I reconstructed service histories and clinician reports overnight, isolated a shared valve batch, and proposed a focused field check that confirmed worn valves.
What was the intended result?
To turn scattered complaints into a testable inspection scope.
I sent three hospitals the standard follow-up form on Monday.
Did you assess their devices?
No, I only requested the listed records.
I archived last cycle's notes on the safety inbox and set up the new folder.
A fresh start?
As fresh as these things get.
The regulator call starts at 09:00, and hospitals must receive a holding message by 09:30.
Are those deadlines fixed?
Yes, they are on the liaison schedule.
A vendor call about the complaint chronology ran long but ended well.
Worth the time?
This one, yes.
I walked through the vigilance office checklist with the new starter.
How did they do?
Careful and quick, a good sign.
Quiet afternoon; I cleared the backlog around the recall alerts.
A rare day.
I did not waste it.
I flagged a small inconsistency in the safety inbox records and fixed it at the source.
Root cause or symptom?
Root cause, for once.

In an April rapid-recall huddle, I acted as the initial hazard voice and attributed alarms to a battery lot from one hospital report; maintenance records later tied them to a software update, and unaffected units were held.
What were you expected to provide?
A live causal position before the complaint histories had been reconciled.
I sketched next week's plan for the recall alerts before leaving.
Ahead of schedule?
Ahead enough to sleep well.
Lunch walk, then a clean pass through the complaint chronology updates.
Does the walk help?
It resets the afternoon.
The overnight review room is available until 08:30, and the call agenda has separate evidence-summary and initial-hazard slots.
Is that division permitted?
Yes, both slots are on the approved agenda.
I compared two options for the safety inbox tooling and noted a mild preference.
Decision made?
Deferred until the trial ends.
I closed the week by updating the vigilance office handover notes.
Anything unusual to hand over?
Blessedly little.
The liaison asks me to rank the two regulator-call duties. Should initial hazard spokesperson come first?
